title: The client runtime is not built; each of its guarantees is restated on the host
Features place UI through a host-side region registry, and one state element tells open pages when the composition or the release changed
One page shell and one view contract: a view gets data, a page is complete without script, untrusted markup is always fenced
One first-party script with a fixed list of jobs; islands are declared by components and framed when they need more than the base policy
Browser-side state has four homes, and only shortcut overrides are stored per device
Shortcuts are commands registered on the host and dispatched from a rendered table; overrides stay on the device; the browser's own keys stay with the browser
UI text comes from a message catalogue resolved per request; English and Chinese are complete; data is never translated
A file is uploaded when it is picked, as one streamed request, and a staged file is as durable as the draft that names it
Usage events are recorded on the host from a closed catalogue, and nothing is sent until the user opts in
Every page is one complete document in one shell, written against one view contract
A feature contributes UI to a place it does not own, and its UI leaves with it, in open pages too
An open page stays connected, says what state it is in, and loses nothing the user typed
A component can ship a browser widget that loads only when shown and cleans up when removed
Collapsed panels, pane sizes, scroll positions and unsent text survive swaps, reloads and other tabs
The UI can be driven from the keyboard, with shortcuts a person can change on their device, and focus that survives live updates
The UI speaks English and Chinese, chosen per request
A person can add files and images to a message by picking, dropping or pasting, and sees progress
The UI also speaks upstream's six further languages
The six further languages are offered with their names and directions, keep the English placeholders and fall back to English
Usage of the shell can be counted, by a user who opted in
Every page renders inside the one layout with its landmarks, base element, language, locked htmx configuration and document-relative references
With every script removed a session page still shows the transcript and a working prompt form
Templates hold no literal product text, use only the shared helpers, and sanitised content is always inside an hx-disable container
Region registry rules: ownership failures at load, list order, election by phase then priority, keyed dispatch, wrap nesting
Through the real loader, disabling a component removes its contributions, commands and islands and bumps the epoch once
A failing contribution is contained, and the state route answers the current epoch and release
Embedded scripts match their manifest, the first-party script is under its size cap with no evaluation, and islands are served under their declared policy
The layout carries the reconnect settings and all connection-state markup, and every live region can fetch itself
A host preference set in one request is rendered for the same principal on another connection and validated by its declared type
Shortcut commands: duplicate ids and overlapping defaults fail, the table is per platform and holds keys not text, a command leaves with its owner
Every rendered page has a skip link, one main landmark, a polite live region, named controls and ids on focusable elements in swap targets
English and Chinese hold every message key with equal placeholders; language choice, plural forms and direction are correct
A malformed language pack is rejected whole and cannot replace a built-in language
The upload control contains a working plain form and renders its limits; a multi-file post yields one chip per file and a cut-off body yields none
A fresh home sends no usage event; with a permit only declared events with enumerated fields and no identity leave
Every state source behind a live region stops its goroutines within a deadline after stop
A feature appears and disappears in an open page, and a new release is announced
A page reconnects through every kind of interruption without losing input or layout
Islands load on demand, and the keyboard reaches everything
The UI switches to Chinese, and files are uploaded with progress and survive a reload
Language matching and plural selection for the message catalogue (golang.org/x/text: language, feature/plural)
verified: go list -m -json golang.org/x/text@latest, then LICENSE, language/match.go (MatchStrings, NewMatcher) and feature/plural/plural.go (Rules.MatchPlural) read in the module cache; no import of C in either package; 2026-11-18

reason: The package is types for live host config fields handed to browser plugins. No plugin code runs in the page: a Go component reads its own typed config struct, renders from the current value, and calls Shell.Touch when a live field changes so that open pages refresh their regions. The guarantee kept is that a config change shows without a reload and a secret never reaches the browser.

The host half (source check, authentication provider registry, request bridge) is area A18's admission pipeline, used as written. The browser half (generations, jittered reconnect, offline handling, a reconnect command) becomes the stream and conn modules of the first-party script on top of A19's cursor resume. Kept guarantees: nothing falls between baseline and live updates, the page reconnects by itself and shows its state, and typed input is not lost.

Upload when picked, one first-in-first-out queue, progress, cancellation and a reference that a later prompt cites are kept. The carrier is a plain multipart form to A19's upload route with an optional island; the Worker is not needed because the browser streams a File body from disk, and staged references become durable through A07's draft record.

Hot replacement of plugin code has no subject: code changes only with the binary. The other half of the package, keeping open pages in step when a plugin is enabled, disabled or reconfigured, is kept by the composition epoch: a change is published in a state region and open pages re-fetch their regions. The development loop is DevDir, which re-reads templates and assets on each request.

The catalogue with Chinese and English as required baselines, a host-stored preference, browser-language fallback and language packs are kept. Text is resolved on the host per request instead of in the browser, plural forms and direction are added, and the six further shipped languages and packs are P2 data files.

The host half composed a boot graph of plugin bundles and served them; the browser half was a lazy module table. Both exist to load plugin code into the page. The Go replacement is the page shell with embedded, content-addressed assets and a small island table: the only modules a page loads are the first-party script, htmx and islands that are on the page.

Upstream reports desktop interactions by default with account and device identity and machine facts. The Go design records usage events in the route handlers on the host, from a closed typed catalogue, through area A18's reporting channel, and sends nothing without a permit from the sharing gate, which is off by default. Machine sampling and identity are removed.

Addressable shared live data is kept as a contract, with other parts: an address is the URL of a fragment route, a holder is an interest of the tab registered through A19's Tab.Watch, and the live helper gives every such region an id and the ability to fetch itself. The browser-side registry, cache and hook disappear because there is one host state rendered per reader.

A registry of named script environments for optional client extensions; upstream does not mount it by default and states it is not a sandbox. With no client plugin runtime there is no code to place in an environment. Where a separate browser environment is needed the design uses a framed island with its own policy.

The only provider for the script-realm registry: a hidden same-origin iframe that shares object references with the page. It serves the client plugin runtime, which is not carried. The Go design's frames are real document boundaries with their own Content-Security-Policy and a closed postMessage set, declared per island.

The command registry, physical key codes, per-platform defaults, conflict checks at registration, device-local overrides with save-before-activate and the double-Escape sequence are kept. Commands are registered on the host and dispatched by the first-party script from a rendered table. Desktop profiles, native interception and two-key chords are gone with the desktop application.

The store engine (Zustand and Immer snapshots with optional localStorage) kept view state and mirrors of host state in the browser. Host state is no longer mirrored, and view state goes to four named places: the URL, host preferences, the DOM and a small per-tab store in the first-party script.

The need is kept: a feature places UI in a place another feature owns, ownership mistakes fail at load, and removal leaves nothing behind. The mechanism becomes a host-side region registry with kinds One, List, Keyed and Wrap, election by phase and priority, and contributions that are cordis effects. Store seats, derived props and component factories have no counterpart; a reusable assembly is a view with fragment parameters.

The boot kernel builds the module system, activates every client plugin and only then lets the renderer draw; a boot page keeps failures visible. In Go a page is one complete HTTP response rendered in the page shell, readable before any script runs, and a component that failed to load is listed in the notice area instead of a console.

The lookup trusts a TypeScript type argument because TypeScript erases types at run time. A Go component's config is a struct decoded strictly from its own entry, and no component reads another package's config by name from the browser.

The 300 MiB buffer exists because images travel as base64 inside JSON call envelopes. The Go UI has no such envelope: a form body is bounded by A19's small form limit and decoded strictly, and files and images go through the streamed multipart upload route, which is never buffered whole. This area's upload client sends one file per request from a File object.

Upstream only documents that a plain-HTTP network listener exposes the cookie. The Go listener refuses a non-loopback bind without TLS unless the operator sets an explicit insecure flag, and marks the cookie Secure whenever it speaks TLS; area A18 implements it under the foundation decision cited.

API peers are created by the /connect exchange for scripted callers of the browser RPC gateway. The Go design has no gateway and no such exchange: a program uses the SDK protocol or ACP on stdio, so no lightweight peer record can linger. A browser peer exists per signed cookie and ends on sign-out or expiry.

Upstream leaves revocation to each credential provider and its default provider shares one peer among browsers. In the Go design there is one credential scheme whose cookie carries a browser id, so one browser can be signed out and all can be revoked; the stream client of this area shows the signed-out state and stops sending.

An upload is still one streamed HTTP request per file; a failed or cancelled transfer restarts from the first byte. What changed is the cost of the failure: files are sent one at a time, so only the failed file is repeated, and files already stored stay staged across a reload and a host restart.
justification: Resumable offsets need a partial-object protocol on the upload route and in the content-addressed store, which verifies a digest over the whole object. On loopback an upload is a local copy; the limit is felt only on a remote link with large files. Area A19 carries the same limit for its route.

reason: The limit comes from accepting a ReadableStream, which is consumed once. The Go upload client accepts only File objects from an input, a drop or a paste; a File can be read again, so a retry re-sends the same object without the caller creating anything.

A stream has no length, so its progress has no total. Every upload in the Go UI is a File with a known size, sent by a request whose upload progress events carry loaded and total, so each row shows a real fraction.

The Worker is emitted from a function string because the upstream bundler (tsdown) has no separate Worker entry for it. The Go UI has no bundler and no upload Worker: the upload module is an ordinary ES module file embedded in the binary.

The limit describes what re-executing a React plugin bundle does to component state. No bundle is re-executed in the Go UI. The related user-visible concern, that a region refresh must not undo what the user did, is answered separately by the keep and focus rules of the first-party script and by hx-preserve.

Upstream tears the old plugin instance down before the replacement is known to work. In the Go design a region refresh is a request: if it fails, nothing is swapped, the old HTML stays on the page, and a notice offers a reload. On the host a component that fails to load leaves its siblings running and is listed.

Upstream's update stream runs on plugins that can themselves be replaced, so a failed replacement of the carrier ends updates until reload. The Go stream client is a static file that is never replaced in a running page, it retries without end, and before each new stream it asks the state route, which also reports a release change.

Upstream registries capture translated text at registration, so it keeps the old language. In the Go design a registration (a command label, a region title, an island fallback) stores a message key, and the text is looked up in the request's language each time a response is rendered. A test rejects literal text in templates.

Upstream leaves plural rules and bidirectional layout to each language pack. The Go catalogue selects the plural form of a message from the first integer argument with the plural rules of golang.org/x/text, and the shell sets the dir attribute from the language, so a pack supplies data only. Right-to-left styling itself is area C2's use of logical CSS properties.

Revisions from file modification time and size exist because plugin bundles are files rebuilt on disk by the npm build and re-served. Go assets are embedded in the binary and addressed by the SHA-256 of their content; nothing is rebuilt under a running host.

The flat module graph is a property of the browser-side CommonJS module table for plugin bundles. The Go UI has no module graph of its own: the first-party script and each island are plain ES modules that the browser links.

Upstream learns of a new host release only from one stream that can fail for good. In the Go design the release identity is in the state region that every stream connect sends as a baseline, and in the answer of GET /ui/state, which the script requests before every reconnect; the stream client never gives up.

The missing commit is a consequence of launching the host from TypeScript source without a build step. A Go binary always carries its version and source revision in its build information, which is where the release identity is read from.

The limit is about replacing the module bootstrap and package code inside a running page, which exists only because plugin code is loaded at run time. The Go design replaces no code in a page: code changes with the binary, and a page then shows a reload prompt.

The retained response bodies belong to the bundle server and its one-generation tolerance for hot replacement. Go assets are served from the embedded file system with no per-request body cache and no generations.
Source maps of rebuilt plugin bundles are an artefact of the upstream JavaScript build. The first-party script is shipped as written, unminified and without a source map.

The unobserved edit is to an npm package manifest and to Node's package configuration cache. No package manifest describes UI contributions in Go: a component registers its regions, islands and commands in code when it loads.

The cause is the desktop forwarder that rewrites cache headers to no-store. There is no desktop application and no forwarder; asset URLs carry a content hash, so the browser may cache them for as long as it likes.

The one-shot environment sample exists to attach processor, memory and operating-system build facts to every event. The Go design attaches none of them, so nothing is sampled and nothing can time out; the resource is the service name and version, operating-system family, architecture and an anonymous installation id.
The fixed PowerShell queries gather the machine facts of the previous unit. With no machine sampling there is no query for a managed Windows machine to block.

Upstream's switch stops collection but queued records are still exported. In the Go design a sender works only while it holds a permit from area A18's sharing gate, and the permit's context ends the moment the setting is turned off or the off-switch is set, so queued records are dropped, not flushed.

Half is removed: there is no renderer-side sender whose failure could be discarded, because events are recorded in host handlers. The other half stays: the reporting channel is memory-only with no acknowledgement from a warehouse, so events are lost on overflow, failure and exit; the loss is counted and shown.
justification: A durable outbox would keep usage data on disk and would have to be purged whenever consent is withdrawn; area A18 decided against it for every reporting channel. Usage counts are best effort by nature and nothing in the product depends on them.

reason: The limit is about a native desktop launcher that must wait for the host before it can report its own start. There is no native launcher: the host is the only process, and a start that fails is recorded by the local fatal diagnostic, not by analytics.

Upstream keeps a record in the page for every address ever read. In the Go design the browser holds no records: a held address is an interest in the host's tab record, which is capped per tab, removed when the region is closed and dropped a short time after the tab's last stream ends.

Upstream relies on each provider to honour its abort signal. Sources are now compiled-in Go components, not third-party browser code, and a conformance test runs every state source behind a live region under a leak check that fails if work continues after stop, so the convention is enforced.

The limit describes a same-origin iframe used as a script environment for client plugin code, which exists only because plugins run in the page. The Go design runs no plugin code in the browser; its frames are for vendored island code and carry their own Content-Security-Policy.

Isolation requests, capability matching and plugin placement are deferred features of an environment registry for client plugin code. With no JavaScript plugin runtime in the browser there is nothing to place or isolate; untrusted code runs in plugin processes on the host.

The bullet records that web defaults must avoid chords the browser keeps (so Mod+Alt and Mod+Shift forms are used and some commands are unbound). That stays true: a page cannot receive a chord the browser reserves. The Go UI declares web defaults per platform under the same constraint and gives every command a visible control.
justification: This is a limit of the web platform, and the owner removed the desktop application whose native interception lifted it. An installed web app window frees some chords in some browsers, which cannot be relied on.

reason: Upstream persists view state as JSON in localStorage, so it differs per browser profile. Preferences that shape rendering are now stored by the host per principal and rendered into the first response, so every tab and browser of that principal agrees; only shortcut overrides stay on the device, by decision.
The bullet is about how the store library is fed to the Vite build and when Immer freezes snapshots. Neither Vite nor the store engine exists in the Go design.

The linear scan is in the TypeScript ledger that answers whether an entry is live. The Go registry keeps contributions in a map by region and removes each through its own effect cleanup, so liveness is never searched for.
The phantom type member exists to make TypeScript compare generic method signatures strictly. Go has no counterpart; region ownership is checked at load by the registry.

Upstream reports an optional plugin's boot failure only in the browser console. In the Go design a component that fails to load is a failed fiber on the host; the shell contributes a notice for the owner that names the count and links to the inventory, and the page itself renders without that component's regions.

The waterfall let a plugin refuse or hold authenticated requests before the body was read; upstream's desktop used it to lock new work during an approved installation. There is no desktop installer, and area A18's admission pipeline deliberately has no middleware seat, so no Go event replaces it.

The schema splits three ways. recovery becomes shell.Config.Reconnect with the same caps, rendered into the page for the stream client. trustedHosts is area A18's listen.Config.TrustedHosts. maxRequestBodyBytes becomes A19's web.Config.MaxFormBytes for form bodies and area A07's attachment limit for uploads.

pollIntervalMs sets how often rebuilt bundles are looked for. Nothing is rebuilt under a running Go host. The development equivalent is shell.Config.DevDir, which re-reads templates and assets from a directory on each request and needs no interval.

enabled, which defaults to true upstream, is replaced by area A18's report.Config.Analytics.Enabled, which defaults to false and is shown in settings. appVersion comes from the binary. The two environment-query fields are gone because nothing samples the machine.
The one field, stopSequenceMs, becomes keys.Config.StopSequence, a live duration with the same 500 ms default, rendered into the shortcut table so that the script can time the double-Escape sequence.

ctx.clientModules composes the boot graph of client bundles and serves them. The Go service that stands in its place is shell.Key (interface Shell): it owns the layout, the region registry and the island table, and composes no bundle graph because pages are rendered on the host.
ctx.config exists in the browser to read another package's synced config. No Go service replaces it: there is no browser plugin, and a component reads only its own typed config struct on the host.

ctx.connection joins the transport, the source check, peer creation and the authentication registry. On the host those are area A18's listen.Key and its listen.Authenticate key; in the browser the connection is the stream client of the first-party script, which is not a service.

ctx.fileUploads owns the streaming route and an in-memory table of staged receipts per session. The route is A19's session.upload over A07's attachments.Store, and the receipt table becomes the session's draft record in A07's store, so no separate service remains; this area supplies the upload control.

ctx.productAnalytics takes events from the renderer and the desktop shell and adds identity and machine facts. Its replacement is area A18's report.Key (interface Reporter): a typed, closed catalogue that route handlers report to and that sends only with a permit.

Final verdict after reading the note: keep its four answers in host form, drop the mechanism. Who may render into a place is enforced at load by Declare and Contribute; a component stays a pure function because a view gets typed data and no service; lifetime is the cordis effect; view state moves to the four named places. The single register call, the four props shares and the store seat exist for React and are not carried.

Final verdict: the first verdict stands. The note gives the browser a module system and the vendored loader so that client plugins load, unload and hot-reload like host plugins. No plugin code runs in a Go page; the host loader already governs every component, and what users saw of it (features come and go without a reload) is kept by contributions as effects and the composition epoch.

Final verdict: keep the rule that browser trust is enforced once for every route, with one change the first verdict missed. The authority fence (Host must be loopback, the bind address or a trusted host) is kept by area A18. The media-type fence (every POST must be JSON) cannot be kept, because an HTML form posts content types that a cross-site page may send without a preflight; the cross-site defence is therefore the origin check, SameSite=Strict and the standard library's cross-origin protection on state-changing methods.

Final verdict differs from the first: not applicable, not replaced. The note defines four build layers and what a JavaScript bundler may inline or keep external so that module identities are shared. It exists only because of the npm build and run-time module loading; the Go UI has one layout template, embedded files and no bundler.

Final verdict: the layering controller, adapter, renderer, component collapses because the host holds the state and renders it. Two rules are kept: each kind of state has one owner, and presentation receives data and never a service or the cordis context. They become the view contract (typed data in, HTML out) and the rule that a contribution closes over its own component's services.

Final verdict differs from the first in kind: ported. All four rules are kept as written: the catalogue owns every product-written string including accessibility names; shared building blocks take their text from the caller and have no built-in language; display text is never an identity; and a source check enforces it. The check becomes a test over templates, and text is resolved per request on the host.

Final verdict: the constraint behind the note is kept (a tab record or link holds only an address, and a view rebuilds itself from it). An address is now the URL of a fragment route; sharing one stream per address and pinning become interests of the host's tab record; the live helper makes every such region able to fetch itself. The browser registry, the hook and its page-lifetime records are not carried.

Final verdict: a factory exists because separately compiled packages cannot pass React components to each other with types. In Go a reusable assembly whose caller chooses inner parts is a view whose data struct has fragment fields, called like any function, so no second registry is needed. Global contributions inside it still use ordinary regions.

Final verdict: adopt, although upstream has not built it. The defect is real (one number decides both whether a candidate resolves a pending interaction or restricts new work, and the order among equals). A region of kind One may declare an ordered list of phases; a contribution names one, and priority orders only within it. Which phases the composer region has is for the areas that own it.

Final verdict differs from the first, which assumed a Go desktop shell: dropped. The note governs which rows of a macOS desktop window can be dragged. The owner removed the desktop application, so there is no window chrome to declare.

Final verdict: keep the web half. Overrides are stored per device in the browser because one host serves devices with different keyboards and reserved keys; a binding is active only after it was saved; an unreadable or newer record blocks editing and is never rewritten; simultaneous writes from two tabs are last-writer-wins. The desktop file store is gone with the desktop application.

Final verdict: the goal is kept (an image is a file fetched when shown and cached by a content-derived name, not base64 inside script). First-party assets are embedded in the binary, addressed by content hash and referenced relative to the page's base. There is no client plugin bundle, and a plugin process contributes no static assets in this design.

Final verdict: the need is kept (a feature becomes an ancestor of content it does not own). The registry's Wrap kind nests each contribution around the owner's fragment, lowest order outermost, with an optional key. Because nesting happens in one render on the host there is no remounting, and a wrapper that fails renders its inner content, which keeps upstream's containment rule.

Final verdict: the principle is kept (a stylesheet belongs to the document and is not a side effect of loading script; one failing sheet must not block the page). Stylesheets are link elements in the page head, contributed through a region, and an island names its sheet in the island table. Module metadata and renderer-side caches are not carried.

Final verdict: keep. The note shows how a credential implementation registers a verifier and owns its peer, while route owners receive the admitted peer and never a token. Area A18's listener keeps that seam as the listen.Authenticate key with the peer in the request context; pages, fragments, streams and this area's routes all pass it.

Final verdict: keep the separation (a reachable address never establishes identity; authentication is its own service; refusal is 401 and a missing verifier is 503). Area A18 implements it with one cookie scheme and a per-browser peer; the first-accepting order among several providers has one member today. The stream client of this area relies on the 401 answer to show the signed-out state.

Final verdict: the two guarantees are kept and the channel is not. A config change shows in open pages without a reload because views render from current config and a component whose output depends on a live field calls Shell.Touch, which refreshes regions. A secret never reaches the browser because nothing is projected to it: a view shows only what it chooses and the secret type prints a redaction.

Final verdict: keep. Files are uploaded in the background as soon as they are picked, through one ordered queue, stored byte for byte once per digest and cited by reference. The storage half is area A07's. Changed here: the carrier is a multipart form with an optional island, and a staged file is kept alive by the draft record, so it survives a host restart, which upstream's in-memory receipts do not.

Final verdict differs from the first in kind: ported in reduced form. A page left open across an upgrade still holds the old binary's script and styles. The release identity (version and source revision) is sent with every stream baseline and by the state route; when it differs from the one the page was rendered with, the page asks the user to reload and never reloads by itself. There are no modules to pause.

Final verdict: keep. An image is uploaded when it is added through the same queue and route as a file, validated and normalised then, so a refusal appears on the image and a send carries only references. Changed: the staged image is durable with the draft, and the draft's chips are restored after a reload.

Final verdict: the first verdict stands. The proposal moves each browser-side read of host config onto config sync; the code it migrates is the React client. Its inventory was used as a checklist of UI behaviour that depends on host config (reconnect timing, the stop sequence, preview policy, notifications): each is rendered by the host from current config.

Final verdict differs from the first: not taken up in this design, recorded as compatible future work. Upstream has not built it. It is a model-facing tool plus an interaction and a submission rule, which belong to the interaction and conversation areas, not to the page shell. The view contract already allows it: a validated description rendered by a registered view, with no generated code. No deliverable builds it.
